blindSummary:
This state/province offers the closest approximation to pockets of refuge in this country: LGBTQIA+ people migrate there to remake the meaning of home and find spaces where they feel valued, accepted and able to be themselves, even if those spaces are hidden and limited. No local enforcement actions, discriminatory local rules, mass raids or violence waves have been documented against trans visitors, and the island sits outside an international LGBT-rights organisation's eight-state/province set of discriminatory rules. However, the 2026 national criminal code applies equally: a provision criminalises sex outside marriage and cohabitation (up to one year, complaint-based by spouse, parent or child), and broad "indecency" provisions remain; travel guides discourage public displays of affection. A 2025 ethnographic study of trans-women communities here explicitly disputes the romanticised-refuge framing, documenting continued resistance and misrecognition and systemic discrimination even there.

Its position above the country-wide average reflects absent local enforcement rather than a legal exemption. Materially safer than the capital jurisdiction with its hotel raids and discriminatory rules, but not a protected space: the new national criminal code and the 2025 national threat-classification rule create fresh exposure that could be activated in any police contact.
